claims.text: The alloy composition is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a single-phase, solution-annealed solid solution.
Rapid solidification by splat quenching retains a highly disordered structure.
Slow furnace cooling increases short-range chemical order relative to rapid quenching.
Both cooling protocols can produce phase-pure samples that differ only in short-range order.
The degree of short-range chemical order creates atomic-scale obstacles to dislocation glide.
Short-range chemical order alters local lattice distortion.
Increased chemical order makes the energetic landscape for dislocation motion more rugged and raises activation barriers for slip.
Increased short-range order raises lattice friction and impedes dislocation motion.
Increased short-range order enhances hardness and yield strength.
Increased short-range order reduces ductility.
A more chemically disordered state permits easier dislocation propagation.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher hardness than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher yield strength than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have lower plastic strain than rapidly quenched samples.
The predicted strength, hardness, and plastic-strain trends will occur at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under compression at 25 °C or 600 °C and up to approximately 5% strain.
Cooling-rate variation affects only short-range order and does not induce secondary phases or other relevant microstructural changes.
Subtle composition fluctuations or unintended microstructural changes during cooling may affect the mechanical results.
Temperature-dependent recovery may modify short-range order and its effect on dislocation mechanics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is bounded to a solution-annealed state, but the rapid-cooling arm is described as rapid solidification by splat quenching, which is not itself a solution-annealing treatment and may define a different initial state.

The experiment seeks to compare ductility or plastic strain, but compression is capped at approximately 5% strain. Unless failure occurs below that limit, this cap cannot establish comparative ductility or strain to failure.
